steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The five main aims of sentencing are: retribution (punishing the offender for what they have done), deterrence (discouraging the offender or others from reoffending), rehabilitation (reforming the offender to prevent future crime), incapacitation (protecting the public by removing dangerous offenders) and reparation (making the offender compensate the victim or society)

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Deterrence is divided into individual deterrence (discouraging the specific offender) and general deterrence (discouraging others from committing similar offences)

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The Sentencing Council issues guidelines that courts must follow unless it would be contrary to the interests of justice to do so, ensuring consistency in sentencing

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Custodial sentences include: detention for offenders under 18, imprisonment for adult offenders, and life sentences for the most serious offences including murder (which carries a mandatory life sentence)

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: When discussing aims of sentencing, always define the aim and give a specific example of how it works in practice Use the terms 'aggravating' and 'mitigating' factors correctly — not 'factors that make it worse/better' When evaluating a sentence, consider which aims of sentencing it serves and whether it achieves them effectively Remember that murder carries a mandatory life sentence — the judge has no discretion on this, only on the minimum term (tariff) For young offenders, always emphasise rehabilitation as the primary aim and detention as a last resort
